segments.t: KorTTY provides a tabbed terminal interface with support for multiple simultaneous SSH connections, split-screen layouts, and interactive terminal management features. This guide covers tab operations, multi-window support, terminal customization, and advanced session features.
The following diagram shows the terminal tab and session lifecycle, including split-screen and broadcast modes.
Manage multiple SSH sessions with these tab operations:
KTPH002KTPH000KTPH003+KTPH004KTPH001KTPH005 (Cmd+T on macOS) — opens Quick Connect to start a new session

KTPH002KTPH000KTPH003+KTPH004KTPH001KTPH005 (Cmd+W on macOS) — closes the active tab. You are only asked to confirm when there is something to lose: the tab has split panes, or a command is still running (a local shell with a running child process, or an SSH session that is not at its prompt). An idle single terminal closes immediately. The tab's close button and KTPH006CloseKTPH007 in the Dashboard ask the same question. The per-connection KTPH008Close tab without confirmationKTPH009 setting suppresses the prompt entirely.

Right-click a tab, the terminal area, or a server entry in the Dashboard. If the connection is active, it is closed and re-established immediately; if disconnected, it is re-established. The terminal window stays open.

Right-click a tab to assign it to a named group for better organization; KTPH000No GroupKTPH001 takes it out of its group again. The same menu offers KTPH002DuplicateKTPH003, which opens another tab to the same connection.

Interactive SSH terminals share host-key trust with SFTP and the SSH bootstrap used by Mosh. The first connection to a normalized host and port shows the key algorithm and OpenSSH SHA-256 fingerprint with KTPH000NoKTPH001 selected by default. After you verify and accept it, exact matches connect silently; a changed key is hard-blocked with no automatic retry, and the alert offers KTPH002Review and Replace…KTPH003 for a key you have verified with the server administrator. See KTPH004SSH host-key verificationKTPH005.

Opening a same-server or newly selected connection in a split shows a progress dialog while the SSH handshake runs on a worker. The interface remains responsive for both the host-key confirmation and keyboard-interactive authentication prompts.

KTPH000Split Right (new connection)KTPH001 and KTPH002Split Down (new connection)KTPH003 follow your organization's KTPH004server access policyKTPH005 like Quick Connect: if the server you pick or its jump server is blocked, korTTY shows the policy message right away, before it asks for a password or saves the connection, and opens no pane. KTPH006Split Right (same server)KTPH007 and KTPH008Split Down (same server)KTPH009 check the policy again: a tab opened from a saved connection can pick up later edits of it, so if its server or jump server was edited to a blocked one after the tab opened, the split shows the same message and opens no pane.

Some failures are refused outright rather than retried, because repeating the attempt cannot change the outcome — a changed host key, an SSH key file that is missing or cannot be read, a jump server whose stored password cannot be used (for example while the vault is locked) or whose setup is incomplete, a Mosh connection configured with a jump server, or a missing Mosh runtime. The terminal clears and shows the reason immediately instead of working through the retry count. See KTPH000Jump serverKTPH001 for the jump-server cases and the Mosh restriction.

KorTTY's pinned SithTermFX build also includes a reviewed bottom-row boundary fix: moving over a hyperlink or the final visible terminal row no longer asks KTPH000 for the non-existent row at KTPH001.

When an KTPH004establishedKTPH005 SSH connection is lost — network drop, VPN cut, server gone — the tab does KTPH006notKTPH007 close. It switches to a red disconnected state instead: the tab title gets a KTPH000 suffix, the tab turns dark red, a red status bar shows the time the connection was lost, and the terminal cursor stops blinking so a dead session no longer looks alive. Only a normal remote logout (typing KTPH001, or KTPH008KTPH002KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH003KTPH011 at the prompt) closes the tab.

KorTTY notices a silent transport death within about ten seconds: every few seconds it sends an SSH liveness probe (a global request the server must answer, the same technique as OpenSSH's KTPH000) and treats two consecutive unanswered probes as a lost connection. The probe only arms itself after the server has answered once, so servers that never reply to such requests keep their sessions untouched. This is independent of the KTPH001SSH keep-aliveKTPH002 heartbeat, which keeps idle connections open but does not detect a dead one.

To pick the session back up in the same tab, double-click the red status bar or the red tab, or use KTPH000ReconnectKTPH001 in the tab, terminal, or Dashboard context menu. In a split tab, panes whose connection died close individually; the last remaining pane keeps the tab open and carries the reconnect offer.

With KTPH000Automatically reconnect lost connectionsKTPH001 enabled (KTPH002Settings → TerminalKTPH003, on by default), the tab reconnects on its own: attempts start after 3 seconds and back off through 5, 10, 20 and 30 seconds up to one attempt per minute, and the red status bar counts down to the next attempt. A successful reconnect, a manual reconnect, or closing the tab ends the automatic attempts. Permanent failures — authentication, host-key verification, configuration refusals — stop them too, so a wrong password is never hammered against the server. While a KTPH004session journalKTPH005 is running, its red decision bar takes precedence and no automatic attempt starts — the journal asks whether to reconnect and continue or to end with its closing summary. See KTPH006Settings → TerminalKTPH007 for the setting.
Open additional windows to organize connections by project or environment:
KTPH003New WindowKTPH004: KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006+KTPH007KTPH001KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH002KTPH010 (Cmd+Shift+N on macOS) opens a new KorTTY window. Each window can have its own set of tabs and connections.

KTPH000Move tabs between windowsKTPH001: Drag a tab from the tab bar and drop it onto another KorTTY window's tab bar to move that tab (and its session, including any split terminals) into the other window.
KTPH000Reorder tabsKTPH001: Drag a tab within the same window to change its order; the "+" tab stays at the end.

Right-click inside a terminal to open its context menu; in a split tab it acts on the pane you clicked. The menu starts with the editing commands below; when you right-click a link, KTPH000Open LinkKTPH001 and KTPH002Copy Link AddressKTPH003 come before them, and on a link to a file KTPH004Open File in Snippet EditorKTPH005 and KTPH006Copy PathKTPH007 (see KTPH008Links in terminal outputKTPH009):
Copies the selected text to the clipboard and keeps the selection. Greyed out while nothing is selected.
Sends the clipboard text to the session, the same way the paste shortcut does.
Clears the scrollback and the screen but keeps the prompt line. While a full-screen program such as KTPH000 or KTPH001 is running, it does nothing.

Opens the find bar at the top right of the pane, the same as KTPH008Edit → Find...KTPH009 (KTPH010KTPH000KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH001KTPH013, KTPH014KTPH002KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH003KTPH017 on macOS). Type to highlight matches, press KTPH018KTPH004KTPH019 or KTPH020KTPH005KTPH021 for the next match and KTPH022KTPH006KTPH023 for the previous one, and KTPH024KTPH007KTPH025 to close the bar.

Below them come the entries of other features, in this order and some only where they apply: KTPH000Show Menu BarKTPH001 (while the menu bar is hidden), KTPH002Open in Snippet EditorKTPH003, the KTPH004AIKTPH005 submenu, the session-journal screenshot and note entries, KTPH006ThemeKTPH007, KTPH008Terminal EffectKTPH009, KTPH010ReconnectKTPH011 and KTPH012Show Command TimestampsKTPH013. The KTPH014ExtrasKTPH015 submenu at the end holds KTPH016Split TerminalKTPH017, KTPH018Font SizeKTPH019 (see KTPH020Font size and zoomKTPH021) and KTPH022Broadcast ModeKTPH023.

Programs can print clickable links into the terminal with the OSC 8 escape sequence; GCC, for example, can link a warning to its documentation. To open such a link, hold KTPH016KTPH014KTPH017 (macOS) or KTPH018KTPH015KTPH019 (Windows and Linux) and click it: it opens in your default browser, or a KTPH000 link in your mail program. Only KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003, KTPH004 and KTPH005 links open in the browser or mail program (KTPH006 links open as text in the Snippet Editor, see below), and a KTPH007 link may only fill in recipients (KTPH008, KTPH009, KTPH010), KTPH011, KTPH012 and KTPH013.

The same click opens a web or e-mail address that a program prints as plain text, such as the address in a log line, a compiler message or a KTPH000 hint: a web address opens in your default browser, and an e-mail address such as KTPH001 opens as a new mail to it. A full stop, comma, quote or closing bracket right after an address is not part of it, and an address that wraps onto the next rows is found from any of its rows. KorTTY looks for the address only when you click, in the text the terminal shows at that moment, so an address that a program printed in several pieces opens whole, and printing output does not get any slower. It reads at most 16 rows above and below the click (fewer in a very wide terminal) and leaves an address that runs on beyond them alone rather than opening it cut short. What the paragraphs below say about clicking a link and about links that never open applies to these addresses too. To turn this off, clear KTPH002Detect web addresses, e-mail addresses and file paths in terminal textKTPH003 in KTPH004Settings → Terminal → LinksKTPH005; links marked up with OSC 8 keep working.

In SSH and local-shell tabs the same click opens a file path that a program prints, such as KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002 or the KTPH003 of a compiler message, as text in the KTPH017Snippet EditorKTPH018. A relative path needs a KTPH004 and a file extension or a line number, so words such as KTPH005 or KTPH006 stay plain text, and a line and column after the path (KTPH007, KTPH008, KTPH009) are not part of the file name. KorTTY reads the file on the machine the session runs on: over SFTP in an SSH tab, from your disk in a local-shell tab. A relative path is resolved against the shell's current directory at the moment you click (KTPH010 against your home directory), so after a KTPH011 the same text can name another file; the Snippet Editor shows the full path it opened. Only a regular UTF-8 text file of at most 10 MB opens; for a directory, a missing file, a binary file or a larger one KorTTY says why instead. Network paths such as KTPH012 or KTPH013, device paths and another user's home directory (KTPH014) never open, so a click cannot make Windows sign in to a server named in the output. Path links follow KTPH019Open in Snippet EditorKTPH020: the KTPH021enterprise policyKTPH022 that removes that entry turns them off too, its read-only mode keeps the file from being written back to the server, and after KTPH015 or an inner KTPH016 KorTTY refuses to open the file instead of reading it as the wrong user. Mosh tabs have no file links.

OSC 8 KTPH000 links, such as the ones KTPH001, KTPH002 or KTPH003 put on file names, open the same way in SSH and local-shell tabs, but read-only: the program that printed the link chose the file behind its text, so the Snippet Editor keeps KTPH009OverwriteKTPH010 and KTPH011Save as...KTPH012 locked and only lets you save the text as a snippet. Such a link opens only when it names no host, KTPH004, or the host the session runs on: the host the tab connected to, the host its prompt shows, or for a local shell the name of this computer (a short name such as KTPH005 matches KTPH006). A link to another host, to a network share (KTPH007) or with control characters in its path does not open, and in Mosh tabs every KTPH008 link stays plain text.

A link opens only on a single KTPH009KTPH000KTPH010 / KTPH011KTPH001KTPH012 click that does not move the mouse between pressing and releasing the button. A plain click on a link does nothing, so a click that only puts the focus into a pane never opens a page. A double-click on a link selects its word and a triple-click its line, as on other text, and neither a KTPH013KTPH002KTPH014 / KTPH015KTPH003KTPH016 double-click nor a selection you drag across the screen opens the link it ends on. KTPH017KTPH004KTPH018+KTPH019KTPH005KTPH020 and a click does not open a link either, because Windows reports KTPH021KTPH006KTPH022 as KTPH023KTPH007KTPH024+KTPH025KTPH008KTPH026. The modifier click also works while a program such as tmux or vim uses the mouse.

Every other link stays plain text and does nothing when clicked: KTPH000, KTPH001 and KTPH002 links, KTPH003 links with any other field (some mail programs attach the local file an KTPH004 field names), and links that contain spaces, control characters or invisible direction-changing (bidi) characters or are longer than 8 KB. Whatever prints a link chooses where it points — a server, a log file you KTPH005, a program's output — so KorTTY never passes a link to the operating system's file opener, which would start programs and scripts: a file only ever opens as text in the Snippet Editor.

Linked text is drawn in the colors the program chose for it, not in the terminal's default text color, and is underlined while the mouse is over it. Two limits remain on screen: a color change in the middle of a link is ignored, and bold, italic and inverse video are not shown on linked text. KTPH000Terminal recordingsKTPH001 keep the bold and inverse video of linked text.

Rest the mouse on a link to see where it goes before you open it. The pointer turns into a hand and the link is underlined, a web or e-mail address printed as plain text included, and after half a second a tooltip shows KTPH006Cmd+click to openKTPH007 (macOS) or KTPH008Ctrl+click to openKTPH009 (Windows and Linux) and the address the link really opens. For a file the tooltip says KTPH010Cmd+click to open in the Snippet EditorKTPH011 or KTPH012Ctrl+click to open in the Snippet EditorKTPH013 and shows the path, or for an OSC 8 KTPH000 link its full KTPH001 target. For a link marked up with OSC 8 the tooltip is the only place that shows its target, because the program can print any text it likes for it. The tooltip writes an international host name in its KTPH002 form, so a letter from another alphabet that only looks like a Latin one stands out, and it shows spaces, control characters and invisible direction-changing (bidi) characters as KTPH003 codes; a very long address is shortened at the end, but its host is always shown in full. An address KorTTY does not open, such as an e-mail link with an KTPH004 field or a KTPH005 link to another host, gets no hand, and its tooltip says that KorTTY does not open it. The underline and the tooltip disappear when you move off the link, drag a selection, scroll, type or switch to another window, and they follow the text when new output moves it.

When the text of an OSC 8 link is itself a web address on another host than the link opens, for example KTPH000 printed for a link to KTPH001 or to a KTPH002 path, a KTPH007KTPH004KTPH008 / KTPH009KTPH005KTPH010 click asks before it opens the link. The question names the host the text shows and the address the link opens, in the same form as the tooltip, and KTPH011CancelKTPH012 is the default button, so pressing KTPH013KTPH006KTPH014 does not open the link. Host names are compared without regard to case, a final dot or a leading KTPH003, and a link whose text is not a web address, such as a word or a file name, never asks.

Instead of holding a key you can right-click a link: the context menu then starts with KTPH009Open LinkKTPH010 and KTPH011Copy Link AddressKTPH012. KTPH013Open LinkKTPH014 opens the link exactly as a KTPH015KTPH005KTPH016 / KTPH017KTPH006KTPH018 click does, including the question above for a link whose text shows another host. KTPH019Copy Link AddressKTPH020 copies the address to the clipboard: for an OSC 8 link the address it really opens, in the form your browser receives (an international host name in its KTPH000 form, as in the tooltip, but never shortened), not the text the program printed for it; for a web or e-mail address printed as plain text the address as printed, so an e-mail address is copied without KTPH001. With the enterprise policy's KTPH021internal clipboard modeKTPH022 the address stays inside KorTTY. On a link to a file the two entries are KTPH023Open File in Snippet EditorKTPH024, which opens it as a KTPH025KTPH007KTPH026 / KTPH027KTPH008KTPH028 click does, and KTPH029Copy PathKTPH030, which copies the path without a line number after it; for an OSC 8 KTPH002 link that is the path the link really opens, not the text the program printed. The menu acts on the link under the pointer at the moment you pressed the right mouse button, so new output that arrives before the menu opens does not change it, and it works while a program such as tmux or vim uses the mouse. A link that KorTTY does not open, such as an e-mail link with an KTPH003 field or a KTPH004 link to another host, gets neither entry.

Quick select copies or opens what the terminal shows without the mouse. Press KTPH010KTPH000KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH001KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH002KTPH015 (macOS) or KTPH016KTPH003KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH004KTPH019+KTPH020KTPH005KTPH021 (Windows and Linux), or choose KTPH022Edit → Quick SelectKTPH023: KorTTY puts a box around every web address, file path, e-mail address, UUID, IP address (IPv4 with an optional port, and IPv6), git commit hash and number of four or more digits that the focused pane shows, and a label of one or two letters over its first characters. Type a label to copy its text to the clipboard; KTPH024CopiedKTPH025 shows over it for a moment. Hold KTPH026KTPH006KTPH027 while you type the label's last letter to open a web address in your browser, an e-mail address as a new mail or, in SSH and local-shell tabs, a file path in the Snippet Editor, exactly as a KTPH028KTPH007KTPH029 / KTPH030KTPH008KTPH031 click on it does; KTPH032KTPH009KTPH033 with the label of anything else copies it like the label alone.

The labels start at the bottom row, so the newest output gets the first ones. Up to 26 different texts each get one letter, home row first (KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, KTPH003, ...); with more, every label has two letters, and the first letter you type hides the labels that do not start with it, while KTPH005KTPH004KTPH006 takes it back. The same text shown in several places gets one label, and at most 676 different texts get one. A letter that no label continues with is ignored. Labels use the keys, not the characters they type, so Caps Lock never turns a copy into an open.

KTPH008KTPH000KTPH009 ends quick select without doing anything, and so does any key that is no label letter, such as an arrow key, KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011, KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013, a digit or a letter with KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015, KTPH016KTPH004KTPH017 or KTPH018KTPH005KTPH019. Clicking into the pane, scrolling, switching to another tab or window, resizing the pane and changing the font size end it too. KTPH020KTPH006KTPH021, KTPH022KTPH007KTPH023 and the other modifier keys on their own change nothing, and holding the keys that started quick select does not start it again. When the program prints over a marked text while quick select runs, that text loses its box and label and the others keep theirs; when nothing is left, quick select ends.

While quick select runs, nothing you type reaches the program in the pane: not the label letters, not the characters they would type, not the text of an input method for Chinese, Japanese or Korean, and in KTPH006broadcast modeKTPH007 not the other panes either. Copies go through KorTTY's clipboard, so the enterprise policy's KTPH008internal clipboard modeKTPH009 keeps them inside KorTTY. Quick select reads the rows the pane shows at its scroll position, the scrollback included when you scrolled back, and leaves out a text that runs on above the top or below the bottom row rather than offering it cut short. It does not depend on KTPH010Detect web addresses, e-mail addresses and file paths in terminal textKTPH011 in KTPH012Settings → Terminal → LinksKTPH013. It needs a terminal tab: in a snippet editor or file editor tab KTPH014KTPH000KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH001KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH002KTPH019 / KTPH020KTPH003KTPH021+KTPH022KTPH004KTPH023+KTPH024KTPH005KTPH025 stays with the editor and KTPH026Edit → Quick SelectKTPH027 is disabled. When the keyboard is in a side panel of a terminal tab, such as the AI chat, the shortcut goes to that panel first, and KTPH028Edit → Quick SelectKTPH029 starts quick select from there.
Adjust the font size of the active terminal on the fly without reconnecting:
Zoom in/out over the terminal (Cmd + wheel on macOS)

Holding KTPH008KTPH000KTPH009 (or KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011 on macOS) and scrolling the mouse wheel over the terminal changes the font size — wheel up enlarges, wheel down shrinks — instead of scrolling the buffer. This complements the KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015 / KTPH016KTPH004KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH005KTPH019 / KTPH020KTPH006KTPH021+KTPH022KTPH007KTPH023 shortcuts.

KTPH000Reset zoomKTPH001 restores the font size and family to what the connection had when you opened the tab (or the connection's saved settings, or the global default). The terminal context menu has the same controls: right-click → KTPH002ExtrasKTPH003 → KTPH004Font SizeKTPH005 → KTPH006IncreaseKTPH007, KTPH008DecreaseKTPH009 (two points per step) or KTPH010ResetKTPH011. The zoom level applies to the current tab — all of its split panes change together — and leaves other tabs unchanged.

KTPH000View → Zoom → Background TransparencyKTPH001 is a slider (0–100 %) that makes the terminal background see-through to the desktop while the text stays fully opaque and sharp. At 0 % the background is solid; higher values let more of the desktop show through. The value is saved and restored across restarts.
Only the terminal area becomes transparent — the title bar, menu bar, status bar and any tab without a terminal stay solid, so the window never turns into a see-through hole.

Horizontal, vertical and nested split terminals inherit the active transparency level, including panes added after transparency was enabled. Entering fullscreen with KTPH004KTPH000KTPH005 or terminal-only fullscreen with KTPH006KTPH001KTPH007+KTPH008KTPH002KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH003KTPH011 temporarily renders the terminal area opaque without changing the saved value; leaving fullscreen restores that value to every pane.

Because a see-through window uses a different window style that the operating system fixes when the window opens, KTPH000switching transparency on or off (crossing 0 %) only takes full effect after a restartKTPH001; the status bar shows a hint when you cross that threshold. Adjusting the level while already in transparent mode applies live. In transparent mode the window uses a lightweight custom title bar (drag to move, buttons to minimise/maximise/close, double-click the strip to maximise, drag the edges to resize).
The slider lives in the in-window menu bar only (the native macOS menu bar cannot host a slider).

Besides SSH and Mosh, a terminal tab can host a KTPH000Local ShellKTPH001 — the local machine's own shell, opened via a pseudo-terminal (see KTPH002Local ShellKTPH003). A few terminal behaviors are local-shell aware:

KTPH006KTPH007KTPH000KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH001KTPH010 closes the tab for local cmd.exe/PowerShell sessions.KTPH011 Those Windows shells do not exit on EOF, so KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015 would otherwise have no effect. For bash-family shells (Git Bash/Cygwin/WSL, macOS/Linux) and SSH, KTPH016KTPH004KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH005KTPH019 keeps its normal EOF meaning — the shell exits and the local tab then auto-closes.

KTPH000Close confirmationKTPH001 uses local-shell wording rather than "End SSH connection?", and the window-close prompt is transport-neutral ("Active sessions"), since one window can mix SSH, Mosh and local-shell tabs.

KTPH004The current directory follows the interactive shell.KTPH005 On macOS and Linux, korTTY refreshes it from the local shell process; native PowerShell and cmd prompts supply absolute Windows paths. After KTPH000, KTPH001, KTPH002, or KTPH003, KTPH006Open in Snippet EditorKTPH007 resolves a selected file name against that current directory instead of the tab's start directory. If the directory cannot be determined or mapped safely, korTTY stops with an error rather than opening a same-named file from the wrong directory.

KTPH006After an identity switch, Open in Snippet Editor is greyed out.KTPH007 When the session no longer runs as the identity the tab was opened with — after KTPH000, an inner KTPH001, or a shell-opening KTPH002 — the context-menu entry is disabled, in SSH tabs as well as local-shell tabs: the tab's tracked directories and file access still belong to the original login and would resolve the wrong path. The entry re-enables on its own once the prompt shows the original user again (typically after KTPH003). A local-shell tab whose configured shell command is itself a remote client such as KTPH004 or KTPH005 keeps the entry disabled for the whole tab. If the load is triggered anyway, korTTY stops with an error instead of resolving the wrong path. The AI context-menu actions follow the same rule: they no longer offer to attach the selected file name's content (see KTPH008Attaching a selected file to the chatKTPH009).

KTPH001Clipboard text is preserved in agent shortcuts.KTPH002 Typed and pasted text travel through the same terminal-input filter, including bracketed paste and split UTF-8 input, so a pasted file name remains part of the KTPH000 request and Enter dispatches it exactly once. In a connection with a single-byte KTPH003character encodingKTPH004 such as ISO-8859-1, every typed character is sent at once.

Every terminal tab can keep a KTPH000session journalKTPH001: server output and typed commands go into a capture log, an AI condenses them into a readable timeline, and screenshots and notes can be added from the journal bar or the terminal's right-click menu. Journals start automatically for connections that enable them, or retroactively for a running session via KTPH002Tools KTPH006 Start/Stop Session JournalKTPH003 — the existing scrollback is imported. See KTPH004Session journalKTPH005.
Split the terminal view to display multiple connections side by side, and optionally send input to all panes at once.
KTPH000Split PaneKTPH001: Create horizontal or vertical splits within a tab via the context menu or keyboard shortcuts.
KTPH000Independent SessionsKTPH001: Each pane can show a different SSH connection.
KTPH000Resizable PanesKTPH001: Drag dividers to adjust pane sizes.

KTPH002Close PaneKTPH003: the × in a pane's top-right corner, KTPH004Extras → Split Terminal → Close SplitKTPH005 in its context menu, or KTPH000 in its shell closes that pane. The × shows only while the tab has more than one pane, and KTPH006Close SplitKTPH007 is disabled in the last one; typing KTPH001 in the last pane closes the tab.

KTPH000Focused paneKTPH001: KTPH002Edit → CopyKTPH003, KTPH004Edit → PasteKTPH005, KTPH006Edit → Find...KTPH007, the AI actions and a recording of the active split act on the pane that has, or last had, the keyboard focus, the one your typing goes to, however the focus got there (a click, a middle-click or a jump from the Coding Agents panel). Closing another pane leaves them on that pane; when the focused pane itself closes, they move to the first remaining pane. The terminal's right-click menu acts on the pane you right-clicked.

KTPH000Access reason asked once per tabKTPH001: when a server asks for a reason for the connection, as a CyberArk-style jump host does, a split does not ask again. korTTY sends the reason that was given when the tab was opened, because a server that asks for one closes a session that answers with nothing. A split to a different server, or a server asking something else, is asked once as well, and a new tab always starts by asking. If the server refuses the reason, for example because a ticket number has expired in the meantime, korTTY drops it and asks again on the next attempt.

KTPH004Move PanesKTPH005: Hold KTPH006KTPH000KTPH007+KTPH008KTPH001KTPH009 (Windows/Linux) or KTPH010KTPH002KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH003KTPH013 (macOS) and drag a pane onto another to reorder. Without the modifiers, mouse drag is used for text selection in the terminal.
When KTPH000Broadcast ModeKTPH001 is enabled, keyboard input is sent simultaneously to all visible panes. This is useful for running the same commands on multiple servers.

KTPH018MirroredKTPH019: typed text, KTPH020KTPH000KTPH021, KTPH022KTPH001KTPH023, KTPH024KTPH002KTPH025, KTPH026KTPH003KTPH027 and KTPH028KTPH004KTPH029+KTPH030KTPH005KTPH031, the arrow keys, KTPH032KTPH006KTPH033 / KTPH034KTPH007KTPH035, KTPH036KTPH008KTPH037 / KTPH038KTPH009KTPH039, KTPH040KTPH010KTPH041 / KTPH042KTPH011KTPH043 and KTPH044KTPH012KTPH045 to KTPH046KTPH013KTPH047, including their KTPH048KTPH014KTPH049, KTPH050KTPH015KTPH051 and KTPH052KTPH016KTPH053 combinations (KTPH054KTPH017KTPH055 toggles fullscreen).

KTPH004Encoded for each paneKTPH005: every pane receives a key the way its own program expects it. When one pane runs KTPH000 or KTPH001, which switch the terminal to application cursor keys, its arrows arrive as KTPH002 while a shell in the next pane gets KTPH003, so history and completion work in both.

KTPH022Kept localKTPH023: the scrollback keys (KTPH024KTPH002KTPH025+KTPH026KTPH003KTPH027 / KTPH028KTPH004KTPH029+KTPH030KTPH005KTPH031, and KTPH032KTPH006KTPH033+KTPH034KTPH007KTPH035 / KTPH036KTPH008KTPH037+KTPH038KTPH009KTPH039 on Windows and Linux or KTPH040KTPH010KTPH041+KTPH042KTPH011KTPH043 / KTPH044KTPH012KTPH045+KTPH046KTPH013KTPH047 on macOS) scroll only the focused pane. A full-screen program such as KTPH000 or KTPH001 has no scrollback, so while one runs in the focused pane, KTPH048KTPH014KTPH049+KTPH050KTPH015KTPH051 / KTPH052KTPH016KTPH053+KTPH054KTPH017KTPH055 (and KTPH056KTPH018KTPH057+KTPH058KTPH019KTPH059 / KTPH060KTPH020KTPH061+KTPH062KTPH021KTPH063 on Windows and Linux) go to that program and, like the other keys, to every other pane.
KTPH000Not mirroredKTPH001: paste and snippets go only to the focused pane, and what you type into the find bar stays in the find bar.

KTPH000A stalled pane does not freeze korTTYKTPH001: the keys for the other panes are sent in the background, to each pane in the order you typed them, so a server that stops responding holds up only its own pane while the window and the other panes keep reacting.

Prevent connections from dropping due to inactivity by configuring SSH keep-alive messages:
Enable KTPH000SSH Keep-AliveKTPH001 in the connection's KTPH002TerminalKTPH003 tab or in KTPH004Settings KTPH006 TerminalKTPH005.
Set the interval (5 to 600 seconds, default: 60).
KorTTY sends KTPH000 heartbeat messages at the configured interval and enables TCP socket keepalive while the option is active.

If a server, firewall, VPN, or NAT gateway closes idle sessions sooner than the configured interval, the connection can still end. In that case, check the server-side SSH configuration and network idle-timeout settings as well as the KorTTY log.

Writes a connection's terminal output to a file, for audit and debugging. This is independent of the KTPH000Session JournalKTPH001: it is a plain transcript with no summaries, markers or screenshots, and the two can run at the same time.
KTPH000Connection Manager KTPH002 Edit connection KTPH003 LoggingKTPH001 for a saved connection.
KTPH000Quick Connect KTPH002 Terminal logKTPH001 for a one-off session, or to change the setting for the connection you are about to open.
Choose a KTPH001log folderKTPH002. Left empty, KorTTY uses KTPH000. You pick the folder; the file names are KorTTY's.
KTPH000Plain TextKTPH001 - One timestamped line per line of output.

Optionally adjust the KTPH000maximum file sizeKTPH001 (default: 10 MB) and the KTPH002retention periodKTPH003 (default: 30 days), and turn off KTPH004Start a new file every dayKTPH005 or KTPH006Compress closed files (gzip)KTPH007 — both are on by default. Quick Connect's Terminal log section covers enable, folder, format and compression; size limit, retention and daily rotation keep their configured or default values.

Every file is named KTPH000, for example KTPH001. The date leads so a folder listing sorts chronologically, and the trailing number distinguishes connections that are open at the same time — two tabs on the same server get KTPH002 and KTPH003 and never write into one another's file.

By default a new file is started KTPH002every dayKTPH003, and always again whenever the maximum size is reached (those parts are numbered KTPH000, KTPH001, …); daily rotation can be turned off to roll only by size. Nothing is ever overwritten or deleted by rotation.

Closed files are gzipped by default; the file currently being written always stays uncompressed so that a crash cannot truncate it. Turn off KTPH000Compress closed files (gzip)KTPH001 to keep finished files as plain text instead. A connection that produces no output creates no file at all.

Files older than the retention period are deleted automatically when a connection starts and after each daily rollover. Set the retention to KTPH000 to keep everything. Only KorTTY's own log files are ever removed — anything else in the folder is left alone, so it is safe to point the setting at a folder you also use for other things.

Captured lines go through the same redaction as the KTPH000Session JournalKTPH001, on the capture thread, before anything is buffered or written: the connection's own password and any replacement rules your organisation's policy defines. The secret never reaches the file, so there is nothing to clean up afterwards.
Log files and a log folder KorTTY created itself are set to owner-only permissions where the filesystem supports it. A folder you chose yourself is left with the permissions you gave it.
Redaction only covers what KorTTY knows

A password KorTTY stores for the connection is redacted. A secret you type into a command yourself, or one a program prints, is not — KorTTY has no way to recognise it. Treat the log folder as sensitive, and use policy replacement rules for patterns that recur.

Terminal recording is designed as a low-resource replay feature. KorTTY records terminal screen-state changes and timing events into one JDK/GZIP streaming-compressed KTPH000 file per terminal tab session. Legacy KTPH001 replay files remain readable.

To enable recording only for this session, open KTPH000Tools KTPH004 Video Manager...KTPH001 and select KTPH002Enable terminal recording for this app sessionKTPH003.
Set the KTPH001Storage pathKTPH002. If left at the default, KorTTY uses KTPH000.

Enable or disable KTPH000Auto-pause when the terminal is idleKTPH001 and set the idle threshold (default: 20 seconds).
Optional: enable KTPH000Capture terminal colors in new recordingsKTPH001 if exported videos should reproduce terminal colors.
Optional: set the KTPH000 path and click KTPH002CheckKTPH003. If KTPH001 is missing, video export stays disabled but replay files remain usable.

While KorTTY renders frames and runs KTPH000, the export progress dialog shows the current phase, progress bar, and estimated remaining time. Export uses the recorded terminal geometry so large terminal screens are not cropped.
